concepts.title: DNA Fingerprinting and VNTR Variation
concepts.definition: People share 99.9 percent of their 3.2 billion base genomes, so Alec Jeffreys' 1984 fingerprinting hunts the variable remainder: tandem repeats called VNTRs - microsatellites of 1-9 bp units and minisatellites of 10-100 bp - are cut by restriction enzymes, separated on gels, blotted to nylon and probed through Southern hybridisation, yielding RFLP band patterns unique enough for forensics, paternity and evolutionary comparisons.
concepts.key_idea: Multiply the genome by the variable fraction to size the discriminating DNA; the band pattern of repeats is the fingerprint.
question_patterns: the human genome spans 3.2 billion bp and varies by 0.1 percent between people - how many base pairs carry the variation
differentiate microsatellites from minisatellites by the length of their repeat units
list the steps of DNA fingerprinting from sample collection to band comparison
why are VNTR patterns inherited and how does that settle paternity disputes
what does RFLP stand for and how does restriction digestion reveal polymorphism
name three applications of DNA fingerprinting beyond criminal identification
why is PCR often combined with fingerprinting of tiny crime-scene samples

solution_steps.explain: Only the variation percentage differs among individuals.
The identical portion is what the variation leaves behind.

concepts.title: Transgenic Plants via Agrobacterium and Biolistics
concepts.definition: Transgenesis plants a foreign gene and watches it pass to progeny: Agrobacterium tumefaciens, the natural genetic engineer, donates its Ti plasmid T-DNA once tumor genes are disarmed and swapped for genes of interest plus markers; where dicots yield to this vector, cereals take DNA bullets instead - gold or tungsten particles shot by a gene gun - and protoplasts accept naked DNA helped by PEG or electric pulses, feeding crops like Bt cotton, grown commercially in India since 2002, along with herbicide-tolerant and virus-resistant varieties.
concepts.key_idea: Disarm the T-DNA, load your gene, and let the bacterium or a gene gun carry it past the plant cell wall.
question_patterns: why is Agrobacterium tumefaciens called the natural genetic engineer
what is disarming of the Ti plasmid and which genes replace the tumor-inducing ones
differentiate vector-mediated from vector-less methods of plant gene transfer
how does particle bombardment deliver DNA into cereal cells that Agrobacterium cannot
which cry genes protect cotton from bollworms and which from corn borers
name two crops engineered for virus resistance and two for herbicide tolerance
how does antisense RNA technology make tobacco resistant to Meloidogyne incognita

solution_steps.explain: Agrobacterium for many dicots, gene gun for monocots and chloroplasts, protoplast methods for regenerable cultures.
Antibiotic or herbicide markers eliminate non-transformed cells during regeneration.
Cry toxins, osmolyte overexpression or viral coat proteins show up as the engineered phenotype.

worked_examples.q: Which soil bacterium donates T-DNA to plants: Agrobacterium tumefaciens or Bacillus thuringiensis?

concepts.title: Transgenic Animals and Molecular Pharming
concepts.definition: Animal pharming turns livestock into bioreactors: pronuclear microinjection into the larger male pronucleus, embryonic stem-cell transfer through the blastocyst inner cell mass, or single-copy retroviral insertion build the transgenics - Tracy the ewe secreted alpha1-antitrypsin in milk, Rosie the 1997 cow enriched milk with human alpha-lactalbumin, and goat-made ATryn won FDA approval in 2009 - while chimeric mice and GEAC oversight frame the research and its ethics.
concepts.key_idea: Inject, electrify or infect the embryo, then harvest the human protein from milk - with regulators watching the ethics.
question_patterns: describe pronuclear microinjection and state two limitations that lower its success rate
how are embryonic stem cells used to build transgenic animals
why does retrovirus-mediated transfer integrate only a single transgene copy
which human proteins have been harvested from the milk of transgenic goats cows and rabbits
what is a chimeric mouse and how does coat colour reveal its mixed cell lineages
which committee regulates GMO manufacture import and storage in India
why was Tracy the ewe an important early success of molecular pharming

solution_steps.explain: Microinjection for random insertion, ES cells for targeted change, retrovirus for single-copy stable integration.
Cultured embryos or manipulated blastocysts go into foster mothers.
Milk-borne proteins are purified for therapy while bodies like GEAC guard biosafety.

worked_examples.q: Which ewe secreted alpha1-antitrypsin in her milk: Tracy or Rosie?

concepts.title: Gene Therapy Approaches and Delivery
concepts.definition: Gene therapy repairs faulty genes by delivering correct copies - the 1990 ADA-SCID treatment of a four-year-old girl set the precedent - through three strategies: replacement or augmentation of the missing function as with CFTR or p53, inhibition of dominant rogue genes by antisense means, and CRISPR-Cas9 editing that snips mutations out; delivery runs ex vivo through cultured cells or in vivo by direct vectors, and only somatic changes stay non-heritable.
concepts.key_idea: Replace, silence or edit - and choose ex vivo convenience or in vivo directness, remembering germ-line edits are heritable.
question_patterns: describe the steps of the first gene therapy performed in 1990 for ADA-deficient SCID
differentiate gene replacement gene inhibition and gene repair strategies
how do ex vivo and in vivo gene delivery differ in procedure and difficulty
why is germ-line gene therapy ethically controversial while somatic therapy is accepted
which protein is defective in cystic fibrosis and which gene would therapy restore
how does the CRISPR-Cas9 system borrowed from bacteria edit human genes
list three demerits or risks of current gene therapy practice

solution_steps.explain: Identify whether the gene is missing, overactive or mutated to pick replacement, inhibition or editing.
Remove-and-return cell therapy or direct in vivo vectors with retroviral carriers.
Somatic edits die with the patient; germ-line edits pass to offspring and demand ethical review.

worked_examples.q: The 1990 gene therapy precedent treated which immune deficiency: ADA-SCID or diabetes?

concepts.title: Recombinant Vaccines from Subunit to mRNA
concepts.definition: Recombinant vaccines trade whole pathogens for precision: live genetically modified or vector-based vaccines such as recombinant vaccinia carrying about 200 genes' worth of foreign antigens; subunit vaccines brewing hepatitis B surface antigen in Saccharomyces cerevisiae since the 1987 Recombivax licence; DNA vaccines shot into muscle by gene gun; and mRNA vaccines wrapped in lipid nanoparticles that powered COVID-19 responses alongside Covaxin and Covishield, with edible banana-based HBsAg vaccines on the horizon.
concepts.key_idea: Deliver only the antigen gene or its message - safer than live pathogen, faster to update for new variants.
question_patterns: differentiate live genetically modified subunit DNA and RNA vaccines with one example of each
how is the HBsAg gene expressed in yeast to manufacture the hepatitis B subunit vaccine
why can vaccinia virus carry genes of several pathogens to make polyvalent vaccines
what protects mRNA vaccines from degradation inside the body and during storage
how does a DNA vaccine delivered by gene gun provoke both humoral and cellular immunity
which Indian COVID-19 vaccines were used and what platform does each employ
why are banana plants considered ideal for edible vaccine production

solution_steps.explain: Live attenuated or vector, protein subunit, DNA plasmid or mRNA-lipid particle.
Pathogen gene to vector to host expression - bacterial, yeast, plant or the vaccinee's own cells.
No live pathogen reactivation, quick redesign for variants, and cold-chain demands for RNA.

worked_examples.q: The subunit hepatitis B vaccine brews its antigen in which organism: Saccharomyces cerevisiae or E. coli?

concepts.title: Monoclonal Antibodies by Hybridoma Technology
concepts.definition: Koehler and Milstein's 1975 hybridoma trick fuses short-lived antibody-producing B plasma cells with immortal myeloma cells using polyethylene glycol; HAT medium kills unfused myelomas and aged B cells alike so only hybridomas endure, secreting monoclonal antibodies aimed at one epitope - later humanised with mouse-human chimeric segments for therapy, diagnostics like pregnancy kits and tumor-targeted drug delivery.
concepts.key_idea: Fuse mortality with immortality: only the B-cell-and-myeloma hybrid survives HAT medium and keeps secreting one specific antibody.
question_patterns: describe hybridoma technology with the role of polyethylene glycol and HAT medium
why do unfused myeloma cells die in HAT medium while hybridomas survive
differentiate polyclonal from monoclonal antibodies on the basis of epitope specificity
what are humanised or chimeric antibodies and why are they preferred in therapy
name two diagnostic applications of monoclonal antibodies
why are B cells cultured alone unsuitable for large-scale antibody production
list the five antibody classes present in human serum

solution_steps.explain: Antigen exposure yields antibody-secreting plasma cells from the animal.
PEG fuses B cells to immortal myeloma cells; HAT medium selects the hybrids.
Screened hybridoma clones supply uniform monoclonal antibody for diagnosis or therapy.

worked_examples.q: Which medium kills unfused myelomas in hybridoma work: HAT or LB?

concepts.title: Engineered Insulin Chain Arithmetic
concepts.definition: Insulin's active form holds a 21-residue A chain bonded to a 30-residue B chain, carved from an 86-residue proinsulin whose 31-residue C chain and four connecting residues are trimmed away; bacteria cannot perform this editing, so engineers clone the A and B genes separately beside beta-galactosidase, release the chains with cyanogen bromide and re-oxidise the disulfides - yielding Humulin, marketed from 1982.
concepts.key_idea: Add the two chains for the active hormone; subtract it from proinsulin to price the editing the pancreas does and bacteria cannot.
question_patterns: insulin has a 21-residue A chain and a 30-residue B chain - compute the length of active insulin
an 86-residue proinsulin yields a 51-residue insulin - how many amino acids are cleaved away in total
how many amino acids does the C chain of proinsulin carry and what else accompanies its removal
why must the A and B chain genes be cloned separately in bacteria for insulin production
which chemical cleaves the beta-galactosidase fusion protein to free the insulin chains
under what brand and in which year did engineered human insulin reach the market
why can pig or cow insulin trigger allergic responses in some diabetic patients

solution_steps.explain: Active insulin is the sum of its A and B chains.
Proinsulin loses the C chain and connector residues during maturation.

worked_examples.q: How many residues does insulin's A chain hold?

concepts.title: Human Growth Hormone Gene Engineering
concepts.definition: Growth hormone deficiency once demanded pituitaries from more than eighty cadavers per year of treatment and risked prion disease, so engineers rebuilt the gene: the cDNA encodes mature 191-residue HGH plus a 26-residue signal peptide, EcoRI excision removes the signal and a further 24 residues, and a chemically synthesised 24-residue segment is ligated back before expression in E. coli - products Humatrope and Protropin from 1985.
concepts.key_idea: Add the signal peptide to size the cDNA product, subtract the excised codons, then add back the synthetic piece to restore the full hormone.
question_patterns: the HGH cDNA codes for 191 mature residues plus a 26-residue signal peptide - find the intermediate length
EcoRI cleavage removes 50 codons and a synthetic 24-residue piece is ligated back - how long is the final expressed hormone
why must the signal peptide sequence be removed before expressing HGH in bacteria
why was cadaver-derived growth hormone treatment risky and costly
under which brand names did engineered human growth hormone reach the market and in which year
which enzyme performed the excision that no other restriction site matched in the HGH cDNA
what deficiency disease does growth hormone therapy treat and at which life stage

solution_steps.explain: The cDNA product carries the mature hormone plus its signal extension.
EcoRI cleavage deletes the signal and extra residues together.
A chemically made segment is ligated back to complete the gene.

worked_examples.q: How many residues long is mature human growth hormone: 191 or 26?
